li.a: The Korea Times (2011): Compensation claim period limitless for inhumane state crimes
Maeil Shinmun (2002): Revealing the Korean War civilian massacres, part 2, the army and police's lawlessness
Kyunghyang Weekly (2023): Series on past state crimes, part 15, the bloody Christmas of a mountain village
Korea University research repository (2011): Characteristics of civilian massacres in the Daegu-Gyeongbuk region before the Korean War
Participedia: Truth and Reconciliation Commission of South Korea
The Korea Times (2009): Government killed 3,400 civilians during war
Associated Press via Fox News (2010): South Korean inquiry into bloody hidden history ends

content.p: On 24 December 1949, a group of South Korean soldiers walked into Seokdal, a mountain village of 24 households in Mungyeong, a city in North Gyeongsang Province. By the end of that day, 86 villagers were dead, and Kyunghyang reports that all 24 houses had burned. The killings took place about six months before the Korean War began in June 1950. Until the official finding of 2007, the account given at the time blamed communist guerrillas.

Seokdal was a mountain village where, according to the Kyunghyang weekly's account, 127 people lived in 24 households. The Kyunghyang series puts the arrival of the troops at about noon. It describes two platoons, some 70 men from the 25th unit of the 2nd Division, sent on a mission the series calls reconnaissance during an anti-guerrilla operation. The Korea Times, reporting the 2011 court case, said that about 100 villagers were shot.

The Maeil Shinmun, a Daegu newspaper, drew on a secret US military document that was released in 1998. In its account, the soldiers gathered the villagers, questioned them about links with communists, and opened fire when they denied them. Those still alive were then shot again. Kyunghyang quotes a survivor's recollection of the houses being set alight from the top of the village downwards, with people ordered out of their homes as the fire spread.

The killing did not stop inside the village. Kyunghyang reports shots at the edge of the village, where children walking home on the school's last day before the holidays were killed, along with men and young adults returning from a neighbouring village. Kyunghyang gives the number of houses burned as 24. The Maeil Shinmun reported that six households were wiped out entirely.

The age profile of the dead is the most striking point in the two accounts that give it. The Maeil Shinmun reported 13 people aged 65 or over, 26 under 15, and 41 women among the 86. Kyunghyang gives a different breakdown: 22 children aged ten or under and 43 people aged 20 or under, meaning about half of those killed were young. Kyunghyang also records that a pregnant woman was shot and survived by pressing cotton quilting into the wound; she gave birth 13 days later.
content.h2: What the army and the press said
content.p: The reason given to the villagers was that they had cooperated with communists. According to the Korea Times, which reported the 2011 court case, the state disguised the massacre as one carried out by communist guerrillas. The Korea Times said that the soldiers had labelled the town a "communist village" after the residents did not welcome them. Kyunghyang reports that newspapers at the time described the killings as the last atrocity of guerrillas who posed as army troops to enter the village and kill and burn.
Kyunghyang also quotes a 26 January 1950 report that the defence minister at the time visited the village school, offered condolences and gave consolation money to help the village rebuild.

Contemporary records from US military intelligence are quoted by Kyunghyang. One intelligence log dated 16 January 1950 says the soldiers attacked the villagers on the pretext of collaboration, and that the unit commander, working with the local police chief, falsely reported to senior officials that 70 guerrillas were responsible. A US intelligence summary dated 24 January 1950, also quoted by Kyunghyang, says the scale of the killings was so embarrassing to the government that newspaper reports were banned, the military commanders involved were punished, and the unit's chain of command was reorganised.

The Maeil Shinmun, citing a US military document, names the unit as the 3rd battalion, 7th company. Kyunghyang gives the number of platoons but does not name a battalion, so the battalion detail rests on the Maeil Shinmun's citation alone.

The national body that eventually examined the killings was the Truth and Reconciliation Commission. It was set up in December 2005 to examine human rights abuses from 1910 to 1993, including massacres of the Korean War period. Participedia, which describes the commission's work, records that it received 7,802 petitions and investigated 1,461 cases of massacre. It began exhumations at suspected massacre sites in 2006, the first time in 57 years that the remains of such victims had been unearthed.

Kyunghyang dates the commission's official finding on Seokdal to 2007. The commission found that soldiers had killed unarmed civilians indiscriminately and without mercy. The Korea Times reported that the bereaved families filed their compensation suit against the state in July 2008, after the commission's fact-finding. No other source opened for this account gives the date of the finding, so the year is recorded here as Kyunghyang gives it.

The commission's importance was wider than one village. Associated Press reported in 2010 that the commission was the first government body to confirm publicly that South Korean military and police had carried out a large, secret killing of political detainees in mid-1950. The Korea Times reported in 2009 that the commission had found more than 3,400 prisoners and civilians killed by South Korean military and police in Busan and nearby areas from July to September 1950.

Four bereaved family members sued the state for compensation, claiming about 1 billion won in total. According to the Korea Times, both a local court and the Seoul High Court accepted that the killings were an illegal act by the state. Both courts nevertheless refused compensation. Their reason was that the five-year limit for such a claim had ended in December 1954.

The Supreme Court reversed that decision in September 2011. The Korea Times quotes the court saying that the plaintiffs had good reason not to have exercised their right to claim, because the wrong had been committed systematically by the state or under its tacit rule. It said it was unacceptable that a state which had covered up the truth and neglected fact-finding should then blame the families for not claiming in time. The Korea Times reported that the court turned down the lower court's ruling. The sources opened here do not report any amount awarded to the families.

The Korea Times noted that the ruling would affect many cases in which lower courts had refused claims on the same time limit. It also reported a similar Supreme Court decision in June 2011 concerning a wartime killing in Ulsan.
content.h2: The wider killings in the region
content.p: Seokdal was one of many killings in the Daegu and Gyeongbuk region before the war. A 2011 paper in the Korea University research repository, drawing on reports from the 4th National Assembly and the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, puts the number of civilians killed by police and army in the region between 1945 and 1953 at around 15,000. The Assembly report lists 5,082 victims, of whom 1,665 died before the Korean War. Most of the pre-war victims were from the eastern Gyeongbuk area near the Taebaek Mountains, and most were killed in 1949, when police and army conducted full-scale search operations.

The paper names Seokdal Village in Mungyeong among the major pre-war massacres of the region. It says the incidents were typically of 20 to 80 victims. The Maeil Shinmun reported that a provincial council committee had received 78 reports of mass shootings across the province.
content.h2: Memory, and what was left open
content.p: The families did not organise until the 1990s. The Maeil Shinmun reports that the bereaved families formed their association in 1993, after civilian government came to power, and held the first joint memorial service that year. Its chairman in 2002 was a survivor who said he had lived only because he was lying under his brother's body.

The commission itself did not last. The Associated Press reported that the new conservative government appointed commissioners who chose not to extend the body's term, and that it closed on 30 June 2010, leaving scores of suspected mass graves unexplored. In its final decisions on the remaining cases, AP reported, the commission attributed civilian killings by US forces to military necessity and found no serious US wrongdoing.

Some questions remain open on the sources. The Korea Times says about 100 villagers were shot, while the Maeil Shinmun and Kyunghyang give 127 residents. Only the Maeil Shinmun names the battalion. The date of the official finding comes from one opened source. Each figure in this account is attributed to the source that gave it.
